name: Oral minoxidil
lead: Oral minoxidil is minoxidil taken as a tablet. At high doses it is a prescription blood-pressure drug (Loniten, approved by the FDA in 1979); at much lower doses it is used off-label by dermatologists for hair loss, an approach often called low-dose oral minoxidil (LDOM) that emerged around 2015.[1][2] People use it to thicken and keep scalp hair, which is the most visible part of a frame, and looksmaxxing communities also discuss it for eyebrows, beard and lashes.[3][4][31]

Its appeal is practical. Topical minoxidil needs application once or twice a day and can irritate the scalp or change hair texture, and reviews note that many patients are poorly compliant with it; a daily tablet removes those steps.[5][8] Reviews of the published literature describe oral minoxidil as effective and generally well tolerated in hair loss, with androgenetic alopecia the most studied condition, while calling for larger randomised dose-comparison trials.[5][6][20]

Controlled trials now exist, including a 2024 double-blind trial in men comparing daily oral minoxidil with twice-daily 5 percent topical solution over 24 weeks, a 2024 trial of 65 patients comparing a low oral dose with topical solution, and trials in female pattern hair loss.[7][8][12][15] Common effects are excess hair growth elsewhere on the body (hypertrichosis) and fluid retention, and reviews describe dose-dependent cardiovascular effects.[1][10] Oral minoxidil is prescription-only and not FDA-approved for hair loss; discussion of buying tablets without a prescription appears on forums, and this wiki does not detail it.[29]
infobox: Off-label (low dose); emerged about 2015, led by Rodney Sinclair and others[1]
Oral: prescription-only (US, UK, Australia Schedule 4); topical over-the-counter in US and UK[1]

paras: Upjohn (later part of Pfizer) began with a compound intended to treat ulcers in the late 1950s. It failed in dog trials as an ulcer drug but proved a powerful vasodilator, and after synthesising more than 200 variants the company named minoxidil in 1963.[1] It was introduced for severe high blood pressure in 1971, when clinicians noticed unexpected hair growth in patients; early haemodynamic and clinical experience with the drug as a peripheral vasodilator was published in 1975.[1][11]

The FDA approved oral tablets (Loniten) for hypertension in 1979. In the early 1980s some physicians prescribed the tablets off-label to balding patients, and a roughly decade-long patent dispute involving Charles Chidsey, Guinter Kahn and Paul Grant and Upjohn ended with a consolidated patent in 1986.[1] The FDA approved topical minoxidil for male pattern baldness in August 1988 under the Rogaine name, after Upjohn's first choice, Regain, was rejected as misleading; a women's version followed in 1991, over-the-counter sales and generics in 1996, and a 5 percent over-the-counter formulation in 1998.[1]

Low-dose oral use for hair loss developed from about 2015, associated with Rodney Sinclair and others, and Wikipedia reports that use rose sharply after an August 2022 New York Times article titled "An Old Medicine Grows New Hair for Pennies a Day, Doctors Say."[1] A 2018 case series of 100 women with pattern hair loss treated with very low oral minoxidil plus spironolactone, and a 2019 study in male androgenetic alopecia, were among the early publications that dermatologists cited.[18][19]

Minoxidil is a prodrug: sulfotransferase enzymes in hair follicles convert it to minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels. How that leads to hair growth is not fully understood; proposed pathways include vasodilation, anti-inflammatory action, Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and an antiandrogen effect.[1][10]

Minoxidil does not act on dihydrotestosterone, the hormone implicated in pattern hair loss, in the way finasteride and dutasteride do. A 2022 review gave the average plasma half-life of minoxidil as about 4 hours, compared with about 4.5 hours for finasteride and about 5 weeks for dutasteride.[10] Wikipedia notes that its hair effects are fully reversible and that it does not prevent hair loss in the long term.[1]

Pattern hair loss in men and women is the use with the most published data. A 2021 review found 17 studies with 634 patients using oral minoxidil as primary treatment, mostly for androgenetic alopecia, and concluded it was effective and well tolerated.[5] A 2020 systematic review of low-dose oral minoxidil in non-scarring alopecia and a 2022 comprehensive review reached similar overall descriptions.[20][6]

Clinicians also use it alongside other treatments. A 2018 pilot study treated women with a combination of low-dose oral minoxidil and spironolactone, and a 2025 randomised observer-blinded trial compared low-dose oral minoxidil, topical minoxidil and platelet-rich plasma combined with topical minoxidil.[19][25] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies on androgenetic alopecia described oral minoxidil among prescription treatments that promote hair growth, within a multifaceted approach.[24]

Case series and reviews describe oral minoxidil in chronic telogen effluvium, lichen planopilaris, loose anagen hair syndrome, chemotherapy-induced alopecia and alopecia areata.[5][22] A European expert consensus on systemic alopecia areata treatment describes it as an adjuvant therapy with limited supporting data, and a case report combined it with tofacitinib for severe alopecia areata.[13][23]

Wikipedia lists beard growth as an off-label use of minoxidil, generally topical.[1] On looksmax.org, users ask what an oral tablet would do for brows and lashes and report results in threads about lashes; replies often point to topical minoxidil or dermastamping for brows and beard and to bimatoprost for lashes.[3][14][31] No published trial has tested oral minoxidil for brows, beard or lashes in people without hair disease.

In clinical practice it is prescribed by dermatologists and some general practitioners after an exam, often when topical minoxidil is poorly tolerated or hard to keep up. A 2025 expert review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology was written by hair-loss dermatologists specifically because off-label use lacked standard best practices.[2] Prescribers commonly screen for cardiovascular history and discuss monitoring for fluid retention and blood pressure changes, and the review sets out how experts use the literature to treat safely.[2]

Forum users describe combining oral minoxidil with finasteride, dutasteride or topical treatments, and T Nation posters on testosterone therapy mention adding it for hair preservation.[33][34] A Swiss Reddit post relayed to Lemmy describes years of oral minoxidil alongside dutasteride and asks whether a general practitioner could prescribe both, illustrating the pattern of obtaining it through ordinary primary care.[36] Results are described as appearing gradually over months, with temporary shedding early on, a pattern Wikipedia also lists among effects.[1]

A 2022 comparative review gave a probable efficacy ranking in androgenetic alopecia of dutasteride 0.5 mg daily, then finasteride 5 mg, oral minoxidil 5 mg, finasteride 1 mg, and very low-dose oral minoxidil.[10] A 2020 open-label study of oral minoxidil in men used global photographic assessment, and a 2019 study examined effectiveness and safety in male androgenetic alopecia.[21][18]

The 2024 JAMA Dermatology trial was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial comparing daily oral minoxidil with twice-daily topical 5 percent minoxidil in male androgenetic alopecia over 24 weeks.[7] A 2024 trial in 65 patients compared topical solution with a low daily oral dose.[8] In female pattern hair loss, randomised trials of 0.25 mg tablets and a 0.25 mg versus 1 mg comparison were published in 2021 and 2022.[15][12]

Hypertrichosis is the most common effect and is dose-dependent, and reviews also describe cardiovascular symptoms and signs.[10] Wikipedia lists low blood pressure, salt and fluid retention, oedema, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, headaches and temporary shedding, and rare serious events such as pericardial and pleural effusion, cardiac tamponade and pseudoacromegaly, which are much less common at hair-loss doses.[1] Contraindications listed include pheochromocytoma, a history of pericardial effusion, and pregnancy or breastfeeding; combination with guanethidine can cause severe orthostatic hypotension.[1]

A multicentre retrospective study of 1,404 patients (943 women and 461 men, mean age 43) treated for at least three months examined systemic safety in everyday use.[9] Minoxidil is highly toxic to dogs and cats, and a case in Toulouse, France, involved a child who swallowed topical solution and had hypotension and tachycardia for about 40 hours.[1]

On looksmax.org, users report bloating and under-eye discoloration at higher amounts, ask how to reduce bloat, and one thread titled with a claim of heart harm describes cardiac worry; these are anecdotes rather than clinical data.[3][29][30]

In the United States oral minoxidil is prescription-only and approved for hypertension, not hair loss; topical minoxidil is over-the-counter. In the United Kingdom the tablets are prescription-only and topical is on the general sales list, and in Australia oral is Schedule 4 and topical Schedule 2.[1] Wikipedia describes newer products in phase 3 development, including an extended-release oral formulation (VDPHL01, Veradermics) and a sublingual minoxidil (Samson Clinical).[1]

Oral minoxidil appears on looksmax.org in threads on dosing questions, sourcing, bloat, brows and lashes, and puberty. Some users advise against it when bloat appears and suggest topical forms or dermastamping, while one reply says it would be reasonable mainly for a very lean user with androgenic alopecia.[3][29] Teenagers, including a 15-year-old poster, ask when to start and how it interacts with puberty.[4][32]

Users also discuss buying tablets from overseas pharmacies and marketplaces, a pattern this wiki records without detail. A Lemmy science post titled "Rogaine in a Pill? Oral Minoxidil Aces Major Hair Loss Trial" drew 97 comments, showing how trial news circulates beyond dermatology.[35]

Controlled trials of oral minoxidil exist for androgenetic alopecia in men and women, including the 2024 double-blind trial versus topical minoxidil, a 2024 randomised comparison with topical solution, trials of low oral doses in female pattern hair loss, and a 2025 randomised observer-blinded trial.[7][8][12][15][25] Observational data include the 1,404-patient safety study and the 100-woman combination case series.[9][19]

Registered studies include a phase 3 trial in female androgenetic alopecia with 520 participants, a planned phase 3 trial in men, a planned phase 3 comparison of topical and oral minoxidil with 200 participants, and smaller early-phase trials in cancer survivors and endocrine-therapy-induced alopecia.[16][17][26][27][28] No trial of oral minoxidil for eyebrow, beard or eyelash growth in healthy people has been published.

timeline.event: Introduced for high blood pressure; hair growth noticed as a side effect.[1]
Haemodynamic and clinical experience with minoxidil as a vasodilator is published.[11]
FDA approves oral minoxidil (Loniten) for hypertension.[1]
FDA approves topical minoxidil (Rogaine) for male pattern baldness.[1]
Topical minoxidil becomes available over the counter in the US, with generics.[1]
Low-dose oral minoxidil for hair loss emerges, associated with Rodney Sinclair and others.[1]
Pilot study of low-dose oral minoxidil with spironolactone in 100 women with pattern hair loss.[19]
Review of 17 studies and 634 patients and a 1,404-patient safety study are published.[5][9]
Use rises sharply after an August New York Times article.[1]
JAMA Dermatology publishes a double-blind trial of oral versus topical minoxidil in men.[7]
Hair-loss experts publish recommendations for safe and effective use of topical and oral minoxidil.[2]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss oral minoxidil as a stronger, easier alternative to topical minoxidil for hair, brows, beard and lashes, alongside concerns about bloat, under-eye changes and sourcing; T Nation users mention it as a hair add-on during testosterone therapy.[3][4][14][29][33]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil is a convenient alternative to topical for hair loss.
claims.believers: Users cite not having to apply a solution and some suggest topical for those who experience side effects.[3][4]
claims.experts: Reviews report it as effective and well tolerated and note topical compliance problems; trials against topical exist, with larger dose-comparison studies still needed.[1][5][7]

claims.claim: It grows eyebrows, beard and lashes.
claims.believers: Forum threads ask how much oral minoxidil would do for brows and lashes and share lash results.[14][31]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists beard growth as an off-label topical use; no trial of oral minoxidil for brows or lashes has been published.[1]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil causes bloating and under-eye discoloration.
claims.believers: Users report bloat and darker under-eyes at higher amounts and say they stopped.[3][29]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fluid retention and oedema; reviews describe cardiovascular effects as dose-dependent.[1][10]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title claims oral minoxidil damaged the poster's heart.[30]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists rapid heartbeat and rare pericardial effusion and tamponade, mostly at higher doses; a 1,404-patient study examined low-dose safety.[1][9]

claims.claim: Teenagers can take it for hair or facial hair.
claims.believers: Posters aged 15 ask how and when to start.[4][32]
claims.experts: Published trials are in adults, with one cancer-survivor trial including teens and young adults; no study of cosmetic use during puberty has been published.[5][26]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil is as strong as finasteride or dutasteride.
claims.believers: T Nation and Reddit users pair it with those drugs and treat it as one part of a stack.[33][36]
claims.experts: A 2022 review ranked oral minoxidil 5 mg below dutasteride and finasteride 5 mg, with the drugs acting by different mechanisms.[10]

claims.claim: It works on a different problem than DHT blockers, so it can be combined with them.
claims.believers: Posters describe running minoxidil with dutasteride or finasteride.[36][34]
claims.experts: A pilot study combined it with spironolactone in women, and a 2025 trial compared it with topical and PRP combinations.[19][25]

claims.believers: Users describe shedding and loss when stopping.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says its effects are fully reversible and it does not prevent hair loss long term.[1]

card.summary: Pill minoxidil at low doses for hair loss; trial-backed and widely prescribed off-label, with fluid-retention and heart caveats.
card.note: Off-label and prescription-only; reported effects include hypertrichosis, fluid retention and rare cardiac events.

quick.overview:
Oral minoxidil is the blood-pressure pill minoxidil used at very low doses, off-label, for hair loss. Dermatologists prescribe it as an alternative to topical minoxidil, and looksmaxxing users also discuss it for brows, beard and lashes.

Reviews and several randomised trials support its use in androgenetic alopecia, though larger dose-comparison studies are still wanted. Results last only while treatment continues.
quick.mechanism: It is a prodrug converted in hair follicles to minoxidil sulfate, which opens potassium channels; proposed effects include vasodilation, anti-inflammatory action and growth-pathway signalling.
quick.risks: Common effects are excess body hair and fluid retention; others include low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, headache and, rarely, pericardial effusion. Forum users report bloating. It is prescription-only and not approved for hair loss, and is toxic to pets.

chain: Tablet is absorbed and converted to minoxidil sulfate in hair follicles
Follicles are kept in or pushed toward the growth phase
Existing scalp hair thickens and shedding slows while treatment continues
angle.text: Oral minoxidil is used to thicken thinning scalp hair and slow pattern hair loss, giving a fuller hairline and crown. Because the effect depends on continued use, hair generally returns to its prior course after stopping.[1] Some users also discuss it for eyebrows, beard and lashes, though trials have focused on the scalp.[31]
